cards.prompt: You have a second DataFrame region_managers with region and manager columns. Join it onto df, keeping only regions present in both.
cards.why: An inner merge keeps only rows whose join key exists on both sides.
cards.whenToUse: You only want rows that have a match in both DataFrames.
cards.commonMistake: Forgetting on='region' when both DataFrames share that column name, causing pandas to try merging on every shared column.
cards.example:
#   region  ...  manager
# 0   West  ...    Priya
# 1   East  ...     Omar

cards.prompt: Same join, but keep every row from df even if a region has no listed manager.
cards.why: how='left' keeps all rows from the left DataFrame, filling unmatched columns with NaN.
cards.whenToUse: The left DataFrame is the one you don't want to lose rows from.
cards.commonMistake: Using the default how='inner' and silently losing rows that don't have a match.
cards.example:
#    region  ...  manager
# 6   North  ...      NaN
# 7   North  ...      NaN

cards.prompt: Merge df and region_managers keeping every row from both sides, and add a column showing which side each row came from.
cards.why: indicator=True adds a _merge column labeled 'left_only', 'right_only', or 'both'.
cards.whenToUse: Debugging a merge — seeing exactly which rows failed to match.
cards.commonMistake: Forgetting how='outer' — indicator=True alone won't surface unmatched rows under an inner join.
cards.example:
#   region  ...  manager      _merge
# 4  North  ...      NaN   left_only
# 5  South  ...     Lena  right_only

cards.prompt: Stack two DataFrames with the same columns on top of each other.
cards.why: concat() stacks DataFrames along an axis (rows by default) rather than joining on a key.
cards.whenToUse: Combining chunks of data with identical columns, e.g. multiple CSVs.
cards.commonMistake: Reaching for merge() when there's no join key at all — concat() is the right tool for simple stacking.
cards.example: # all 8 original rows back in their original order

cards.prompt: Same join, but keep every row from region_managers even if a region has no matching sales.
cards.why: how='right' mirrors how='left' but preserves all rows from the right DataFrame instead.
cards.whenToUse: The right DataFrame is the one you don't want to lose rows from.
cards.commonMistake: Swapping DataFrame order and using how='left' instead of just using how='right', making the call harder to read.
cards.example: # South appears once with NaN sales columns; West/East rows repeat per matching sales row

cards.prompt: Merge df with itself on region (a self-join), with custom suffixes '_a' and '_b' instead of the default _x/_y.
cards.why: suffixes controls the labels appended to overlapping non-key column names instead of pandas' default _x/_y.
cards.whenToUse: Self-joins or merges between DataFrames that share column names besides the join key.
cards.commonMistake: Forgetting overlapping columns get an automatic _x/_y suffix if you don't set suffixes explicitly.
cards.example: # category_a, revenue_a, units_a, category_b, revenue_b, units_b

cards.prompt: Merge df onto region_managers, asserting that each df row matches at most one region_managers row (a many-to-one relationship).
cards.why: validate raises a MergeError if the actual key cardinality doesn't match what you asserted, catching join-key bugs early.
cards.whenToUse: Guarding against accidental row duplication from an unexpected one-to-many or many-to-many match.
cards.commonMistake: Skipping validate and silently getting a row-multiplying merge when you expected one match per row.
cards.example: # succeeds silently — raises MergeError instead if the assumption is violated

cards.prompt: Stack two chunks of df back together with a fresh, continuous index instead of reusing their original row labels.
cards.why: ignore_index=True discards the original indices and assigns a new 0..n-1 range.
cards.whenToUse: Concatenating chunks whose original index values would otherwise overlap or be meaningless once combined.
cards.commonMistake: Omitting ignore_index=True and ending up with duplicate index labels across the combined DataFrame.
cards.example: # index runs 0..7 with no duplicates or gaps

cards.prompt: Add a derived tax column (10% of revenue) onto df by concatenating along columns instead of assigning directly.
cards.why: axis=1 concatenates side-by-side by aligning on the index, rather than stacking rows.
cards.whenToUse: Combining a DataFrame with one or more Series/DataFrames that share the same row index.
cards.commonMistake: Forgetting axis=1 (the default is axis=0), which would try to stack rows instead of adding a column.
cards.example:
#   region category  revenue  units   tax
# 0   West    Shoes      120     12  12.0

cards.prompt: After a left indicator merge, keep only the df rows that had no matching manager.
cards.why: Filtering on the _merge column isolates exactly the rows that failed to match, useful for debugging data gaps.
cards.whenToUse: Investigating which rows a merge silently dropped or left unmatched.
cards.commonMistake: Filtering with a plain NaN check instead, which breaks if the matched column can legitimately be NaN too.
cards.example: # both North rows — no manager listed for North

cards.prompt: Use join() (instead of merge()) to attach manager names onto df by region.
cards.why: join() combines DataFrames by index by default; passing on='region' tells it which df column to match against the other DataFrame's index.
cards.whenToUse: You already have (or can easily set) the right-hand DataFrame indexed by the join key.
cards.commonMistake: Calling join() without first indexing the other DataFrame by the key column — join() matches on index, not arbitrary columns, on both sides.
cards.example:
#   region category  revenue  units manager
# 0   West    Shoes      120     12  Priya

cards.prompt: Merge df and region_managers keeping every row from both sides. Fill in the blank.
cards.why: how='outer' keeps all rows from both DataFrames, filling non-matches with NaN on whichever side is missing.
cards.whenToUse: You need the full union of both DataFrames' keys, not just matches or one side's rows.
cards.commonMistake: Confusing 'outer' with 'full' — pandas uses 'outer', not SQL's 'full outer join' spelling.
cards.example: # every region from both df and region_managers appears at least once

cards.prompt: You have two DataFrames with identical columns and want to stack all their rows together. Which call is correct?
cards.why: concat() stacks DataFrames by simply appending rows; merge() always tries to join on key columns, which isn't what 'stack rows together' means.
cards.whenToUse: Combining chunks of data with identical columns, e.g. multiple CSVs.
cards.commonMistake: Reaching for merge() out of habit when there's no join key at all — concat() is the right tool for pure stacking.
cards.example: # all rows from both DataFrames, one after another

cards.prompt: region_targets has the same regions under a column named area instead of region. Merge it onto df using that mismatched key.
cards.why: left_on/right_on let you join two DataFrames whose key columns have different names.
cards.whenToUse: The two DataFrames' join keys don't share a common column name.
cards.commonMistake: Trying on='region' when the right DataFrame doesn't have a column by that exact name — pandas raises a KeyError.
cards.example:
#   region category  revenue  units   area  target
# 0   West    Shoes      120     12  West     200
